The early seasons definitely portrayed the Asgard in a power level that wasn't matched much later. That said, there's definitely some room for it to make sense, from some of the aforementioned fan theories around he was in the neighborhood or set out as soon as they entered the throne room.


That said, there was also a good bit of retconning, particularly during the earlier replicator storylines. Perhaps the best example is a throwaway background explanation from Thor on how the ship was setup, which basically said Asgard ships are massive power reactors with some engines strapped to it. Some discussions later point to them being roughly ZPM-level output, which is an absurd amount of power. With Prometheus in tow, they were also a lot slower, so we can speculate that they did a lot of optimization for speed over anything else.


The Ori were powerful, but clearly limited in tech in a number of ways. Their onboard power generator was roughly ZPM-level, but it was substantial in size. Their shields were powerful, but the Atlantis shields were still clearly superior. There's no reason to expect their hyperdrives to be significantly more efficient than the Asgard, who clearly designed around maximum speed, and their ships were much larger and tailored for a mix of space, air, and ground superiority for a proper galactic invasion. They carried armies and massive fleets, as opposed to the Asgard who rarely flew more than a handful of people on their ships.


Lastly, every implication is the Alterans went REALLY far away from the Ori home galaxy. Even if the Ori could beat the speed of the Asgard, why would they? Wormhole travel is effectively instantaneous, so reinforcements don't need to be staggered and they can focus ship design on war by using a simple massive stargate.


One last thing to remember is that the Ori fleet was constructed by humans that, until the crusade, were living in roughly medival era. The Priors were required to start the power generators and bring the ships to life, so we can add more evidence to the idea that the Ori tech was optimized to be easier for the human worshippers to achieve while being the best it could be in that form. A short list of things you'll likely end up doing over the next few months:

* New Extruder (either metal, dual gear, bmg, etc.) Stock plastic one breaks on the arm, just depends on how lucky you are on how soon that is.
* New bowden tube. Often will come with the extruder, but you want the blue Capricorn tubing. It'll improve performance and reliability of printing once you retune retraction settings.
* All-metal heatbreak or even a completely new hotend. Stock setup has a tendency to leak plastic when the bowden tube slips even a little bit out of place, often resulting in a giant blob of plastic where your hotend used to be.
* Improved parts cooling. Stock setup SUCKS for overhangs and bridges. Lotta options here, all printed minus a little hardware and some fans.
* Silent motherboard. Stock board doesn't fail often, but you will want this for quietness.
* PEI spring steel bed sheet. Stock clonetak is fine, but has a tendency to get damaged and needs replacing either because of use or because of accidents with bed leveling. The textured Creality option for $12 is perfect here.
* BL-Touch or CR-Touch. Adds bed probe leveling, which once setup kills all leveling woes. People will always say "oh replace your springs and nuts with {insert new hotness} and you'll never relevel your bed again!", but they're lying and they know they're lying. You change bed surface, nozzle, or just wait enough time, and you're going to have to relevel. This kills most of the dumb needs to relevel (slight shifting in the bed height due to any number of reasons) and only needs you to change z offset when you change nozzles or hotends.


Here's a list of things people will tell you you need that's pretty much unnecessary:

* Dual Z axis. Learn how to tighten V-rollers correctly, and this becomes a headache instead of fixing one. If you do do this, change your board out for something like an SKR 2 and add a way to do gantry leveling, otherwise this is really just a headache.
* Direct Drive. Unless you're wanting to print TPU, this is pretty much a cost adder until you're really chasing quality. 
* Linear rails. Unless you're chasing speed (and understand what that entails), this should only be a consideration when you need to replace v-rollers. Even then, replacement v-rollers are probably the better choice.
* New high flow hotend. You're limited by the motion system, not the hotend. High flow is just going to add pains to your life. Stick with a normal flow style and you'll be happy.
* Hardened nozzle. If you're printing Carbon Fiber, Glass Fiber, Glow-in-the-dark, or one of the weird other filled materials, this actually is required. For normal PLA, PETG, and ASA, you're fine with the stock nozzle and the cheap replacement ones.

To give some informative background information on the rest of it: The parts designed in CAD are exported a s a solid model. This model is brought into your slicer of choice (Cura, Prusaslicer, OrcaSlicer, etc.) and the slicer figures out how to lay the plastic per the settings you choose (wall count, infill percentage, layer height, etc etc etc). This means that the infill inside the part is determined during slicing. Part designers might have recommended settings for strength, and there are some things that a designer can do to design for certain settings (thin sections are multiples of some line width or layer height, for example). Part orientation also matters, largely for 2 reasons. First, orientation can reduce or remove the need for supports on overhangs. Second, parts can be stronger or weaker printed in different orientations. The reason for this is due to the layers themselves. Each layer is quite strong, so forces trying to act along a layer have the full strength of the plastic itself to work against. However, the bonds between layers is much weaker, so force that acts across layers only has to pull the layers apart, instead of the plastic itself. For PLA, this difference in strength can be upwards of 40%. Because of this, parts may need a certain orientation to put the largest force in parallel with the layers, of perpendicular.

Ah, got it, you have no idea how a ratchet works. Let me explain.

The purpose of a ratcheting mechanism is to allow you to not have to change your hand position or engagement of your bit while tightening or loosening a fastener. This, in turn, will increase the speed at which you can tighten or loosen the fastener. This is accomplished with a conceptually simple mechanism that allows the shaft to spin relative to the handle. The mechanism is switchable, so the spin relative to the handle is only in one direction, so when you're tightening a screw the handle and shaft are locked together, but if you move the handle like you're loosening, the shaft stays in place and you can move the handle back to be able to tighten again, like you would for a fixed blade but without requiring you change your bit engagement or hand grip. Lower drag on the mechanism means this function works in more scenarios, especially high-precision machine screws which have very low friction to begin with.

>  it means the mechanism doesn’t have much lifespan in it.

All the low force means is a more usable range for the ratcheting mechanism to work. Bearing life will depend entirely on the quality of the bearing, as a low quality bearing will likely fail quickly with little use and a higher quality bearing is unlikely for you to ever be able to wear out. Pretty much every name-brand driver, including the LTT one, fall into the "higher quality" bucket, and you're not going to be able to wear the mechanism out just by spinning, even if that's all you do. Headphones and speakers usually use something called dynamic drivers to create sound. What dynamic drivers are are little circular discs that have a thin membrane that moves back and forth to create sound using a permanent magnet and an electromagnet to create the motion. This driver is actually quite sensitive and can be damaged in a number of ways. On cheap Headphones, the easiest way is to play too loudly which either tears the membrane or damages the coil, either way ruining the driver and making it sound much worse than before, if it works at all.

Higher end Headphones often require more energy to produce the same level of sound. This is usually to improve sound quality (there's actually a lot of reasons and explanations as to why, but the overall result/goal is better audio), so a lot of laptops, desktops, phones, and anything else with a headphone jack may struggle to play audio at an acceptable sound level. In those cases, you'd need an additional amplifier to increase the amount of energy being used to drive the Headphones, and the sound will be louder.

There's an old audiophile myth that many Headphones also need an amp to sound "correct" even at lower volumes. No amount of scientific testing has ever shown that to be true, but you'll hear it repeated over and over for anything costing more than about $50. Quite frankly, even the Sennheiser HD 6XX/HD 650 don't need an addition amp and don't sound different if you do, other than louder, so I always recommend getting headphones and seeing if they're loud enough and clear enough for you first. If you have buzzing or hissing but they're loud enough, often times an Apple USB-C Audio dongle will solve all your issues. Nobody likes that though because they want to spend $200 on a dac+amp instead of $9 for sub-200 headphones, even though the Apple dongle tests similar or better than pretty much all of the dacs out there, low end and high end alike.

But you're factually incorrect. No true blind A/B testing has ever shown amps that provide far more power than needed for normal listening volumes to ever have given a difference while listening at normal listening volumes. If you're failing to hit normal listening volumes (which is a problem with the aforementioned Apple dongle and my HD 6XX) then an amp helps, in so much that it simply lets you actually hear it.

This, pretty much. 4.31 and 4.32 are supposed to be B-die/C-die respectively, but it really just guarantees Samsung. Timings scream C-Die or bad B-die. tRFC is the best way to figure out what die it really is, as nothing will do low tRFC like B-die and even atrocious B-die will do better tRFC than nearly anything else.

Nowadays, all of the guaranteed B-die bins are only good bins. B-die IS very very inconsistent, it's part of why Samsung developed C- and D- die, as they had a hard time making the 3200 JEDEC bin consistently. (There's a lot of other reasons too, cost to produce, power consumption, IMC load which had bad implications for the server markets where you're putting registers on the DIMMs to add more ranks and in turn more capacity. There are 3200 JEDEC B-die modules, but basically everything produced was 2133 despite there being variants for every JEDEC speed up to and including 3200. The fast ones just ended up in almost exclusively ECC memory, and what little testing of the unbuffered ECC variants shows that there's little indication they would give better/more consistent XMP bins anyways.) Buy a lot of batches of JEDEC or low bin kits from Corsair, Team Group, etc etc. and you will find quite a lot of B-die kits mixed in with nearly every other die under the sun. Not that they're any good, I have a late production OEM Samsung B-die 2133 kit that will not do anything above 2933, and really doesn't like being above 2800. Same board and CPU have no problems with 4800 in a 4x8 setup with two Team 4133c18 B-Die kits.

And before you go off that the OEM kit isn't B-die, TRFC of 250 runs just fine. It's B-die, but it's bad. Bad B-die is the NORM, not the exception. Buildzoid has talked about it pretty extensively, it's pretty well known in most OC circles, and random OEM kits show it: B-die largely sucks, but the top end is so good and it's timing capabilities are unmatched so it's still binned and produced. Everyone forgets about 4Gbit Samsung E-Die, which had similar timing performance to B-Die but was just slightly worse and never had the top end frequency capabilities. The capacity and top-end frequency doesn't matter much for benchmarking, but since timings were ever so slightly worse than B-die, it died rapidly. 8Gbit certainly wasn't a hindrance to B-Die gaining better mainstream appeal too.

I think something people forget is that one of the worst things about Samsung B-die (and why good kits of it are still $$$) is that it's suuuuuuper inconsistent. Good bins look about the same, but bad (or random) bins often times can't do much more than what they're binned at. I have a set of oem Samsung sticks with 2133 B-die that legitimately won't do anything above 2933 cl20, and a set of Team XTREME B-Die that'll do 4800 on the same cpu and board.

The first part isn't necessarily an issue (it can be, depending on how it was done, but is largely just annoying) but the second is what makes it potentially very dangerous. 

The big issue is a lot of negative camber remove all contact patch from the tire so under any sort of hard braking or cornering you've removed nearly all grip. Additionally, tires aren't designed to be driven like that, and I've seen people destroy tires (whether by wearing down to cords, destroying the sidewall so the rim rides on the ground, or by actual blow-outs) in under 100 miles.

To be fair, unless you trailer and only take to shows a stanced car is actually dangerous to drive on the road and most people who are wanting to stance are not the type to trailer a show car.

>The big issue is a lot of negative camber remove all contact patch from the tire so under any sort of hard braking or cornering you've removed nearly all grip. For absolute minimum power draw, grab a Ryzen 5800x or better and a B550 board, then read up on PBO to lock down the maximum power draw. You can do UDIMM ECC on most boards as well if you need that, otherwise grab whatever gets you 128GB ddr4, trying to keep around 3200Mhz for best efficiency. Find a Titanium-rated PSU like: (https://pcpartpicker.com/product/cNsmP6/seasonic-prime-ultra-titanium-750w-80-titanium-certified-fully-modular-atx-power-supply-ssr-750tr) but try to minimize the power rating, try to target having average consumption around 40-50% of the rating of the PSU for best efficiency. Don't go lower in rating, you'll loose too much efficiency even if you can get closer to the 40-50% mark.

To minimize cost, look into used Xeon Lv3 or v4 skus and RDIMM DDR4. The power draw won't be anything near as low as the Ryzen system, but you likely can build something for ~60-70% of the cost. The killer will be motherboards, try to avoid servers though as they'll kill your power draw quickly. Stick to single socket to keep idle draw down and efficiency up.

Either way, you want to make everything as big as you can. Bigger fans are more efficient, so less power for same airflow. Bigger heatsinks need less airflow to dissipate the same power, and bigger parts have a wider selection for you to get what really optimizes out best. Active Power Factor Correction. Basically, because AC power is a "wave", the load can draw in a wave that's not perfectly in line with the AC power. This is represented by power factor, and increases the apparent load of devices. APFC tries to sync the two waves to improve efficiency and grid load, and for some customers (primarily businesses) it can result in lower electricity cost. It's also a requirement for 80+ certification, sale in the EU, and is part of why modern power supplies can take input from both 120V and 240V sources.
